summary: Proposes an indexed text encoding for the SIP Common Log Format that keeps the advantages of a text format while making it faster to process. It is the concrete format for the framework in RFC 6872.

eli5.summary: A neat way to write the call-server diary, with a table of contents, so readers can quickly jump to what they need.

questions: what is the sip clf file format
how does the sip common log format work
what is the sip clf record layout
how are optional fields logged in sip clf
subtitle: A two-line, indexed text format for logging SIP messages that stays greppable but skips fast.

tldr.problem: Plain text logs like the Apache Common Log Format force a reader to parse every byte of a log file, which is slow for the large volumes a SIP server produces.
tldr.mechanism: Each SIP CLF record starts with a 60-byte line of hexadecimal pointers to the start of each field, followed by a tab-delimited line of the fields themselves and optional tagged extras.
tldr.outcome: Readers can jump straight to a field, while the log stays human readable and usable with sed, awk, grep and similar tools. The format is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 7355.

facts.label: Timestamp
facts.value: 10 bytes plus 3 bytes of fractional seconds

today: RFC 6873 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7355. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why an Indexed Log Format
sections.content:
The Common Log Format (CLF) used by web servers such as Apache was popular enough that people wanted an equivalent for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). RFC 6872 defines an implementation-independent framework and information model for a SIP CLF. RFC 6873 supplies one concrete file format for it.

The motivation is speed. Experience with Apache CLF showed that large quantities of log data are processor intensive, because a reader has to read and parse every byte of the files it cares about. The new format is described as no harder for a logging entity to generate than a plain text format, but radically faster to process.

It keeps one key advantage of text: records are human readable and can be handled with Unix tools such as sed, awk, perl, cut and grep.
sections.eli5: Reading a huge diary word by word is slow. This format adds a quick index at the start of each entry so a program can find what it wants fast, but you can still read it yourself.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Record
sections.content:
A SIP CLF record is logically three parts, written as a two-line record. The first line holds the <IndexPointers>. The second line holds the <MandatoryFields> and, if present, the <OptionalFields>, ending with a line feed (0x0A).

  • Index pointers: the first 60 bytes. They are metadata that lets a reader skip directly to the field it wants.
  • Mandatory fields: a tab-delimited (0x09) list of the mandatory information model elements from RFC 6872, in the order listed in the pointers.
  • Optional fields: an optional extension for anything not mandatory, including SIP bodies and vendor-specific data.

Numbers described as hexadecimal use the characters 0 to 9 and A to F. Decimal numbers use 0 to 9. In both cases a number always fills the stated number of bytes and is padded on the left with 0 characters.
sections.eli5: Each entry has three parts: a table of contents, the must-have facts about the message, and a box of extra notes you can add if you want.

sections.title: The Index Pointers
sections.content:
The 60-byte index line starts with a Version byte, a letter from A to Z. This document uses A (0x41). The version MUST be incremented for any new SIP CLF specification that changes any part of the record format, and the values are assigned by IANA. Because the version is per record, one file could mix versions, but this SHOULD be avoided.

Next comes a 6-byte hexadecimal Record Length, counting from the Version byte through the terminating line feed. After a comma, bytes 8 through 55 carry pointers to the start of each mandatory field, and bytes 56 through 59 carry the Optional Fields Start Pointer. The pointers are packed together with no delimiters as one 52-character hexadecimal string. They are absolute byte positions within the record, so they are at least 82.

The Optional Fields Start Pointer points at the tab that begins the first optional field. If there are no optional fields it MUST point at the terminating line feed.
sections.eli5: The first thing in each entry is a list of page numbers, one for each fact, so you can open the entry at exactly the right spot.

sections.title: The Mandatory Fields
sections.content:
After the index line come two fixed-width fields for the time of the log entry: a 10-byte decimal Timestamp (seconds since the Unix epoch) and 3 bytes of fractional seconds for millisecond accuracy, joined by a .. Then a 5-byte Flags field follows, one byte each for request or response, retransmission status, sent or received, transport and encryption.

The remaining mandatory fields come from RFC 6872: CSeq, Response Status-Code (a single hyphen character for requests), Request-URI, destination IP address and port, source IP address and port, To URI, To tag, From URI, From tag, Call-ID, and the server and client transaction identifiers. IPv4 addresses are written in dotted decimal and IPv6 addresses in square brackets using the notation of RFC 5952. The data MUST appear in the order of the pointers and every field MUST be present, subject to the 4096-byte maximum field size.

The transaction fields let a reader tie ACKs and CANCELs to an INVITE transaction and follow forking. An implementation can reuse the topmost Via branch value or generate its own unique string.
sections.eli5: These are the must-have facts about each message: when it happened, whether it was sent or received, who it was from and to, and which call it belongs to.

sections.title: Escaping and Missing Values
sections.content:
Mandatory fields are separated by single tab characters. Any tab inside data to be logged is replaced by a space before logging. The RFC admits two consequences: a signature over a logged field cannot be reconstructed to match the original message, and any future SIP header that gives tabs a special meaning would lose it. This replacement also applies to optional fields.

When a mandatory field has no value, it MUST be encoded as a single hyphen character (0x2D). A field that failed to parse MUST be encoded as a single question mark. If the real value is exactly one character and that character is a hyphen or a question mark, the implementation SHOULD write the escaped forms %2D or %3F instead. The line ending after a header value MUST NOT be logged.

The log is not meant to recreate the original message bit for bit. A log reader should never unescape anything, since the records are meant for text tools such as grep and awk.
sections.eli5: If a fact is missing, you write a dash. If you could not read it, you write a question mark. Tabs are swapped for spaces so the columns never get mixed up.

sections.title: Optional Fields
sections.content:
Optional fields may appear zero or more times after the mandatory ones. Each starts with a tab and has the form Tag@Vendor-ID,Length,BEB,Value. The Tag is two bytes and the Vendor-ID is eight bytes, both decimal. The Vendor-ID is either 00000000 for fields defined by this document or a vendor's Private Enterprise Number for vendor-specific data. The Length is four hexadecimal bytes covering only the Value.

The BEB (Base64 Encoded Byte) is 00 if the value is stored as is and 01 if it is Base64 encoded. A value MUST be Base64 encoded if it contains unprintable octets: values 0 to 31, the value 127, or sequences of 128 and above that are not valid UTF-8.

With Vendor-ID 00000000, three tags are defined:

  • 00 logs one SIP header field, or the Reason-Phrase written as Reason-Phrase: followed by its value. Repeated headers such as Via are logged as separate entries in their original order.
  • 01 logs the message body, prefixed by its Content-Type and a space. CRLFs are escaped as %0D%0A. At most one entry.
  • 02 logs the entire SIP message, with CRLFs escaped the same way. At most one entry.

Bodies and whole messages MUST be truncated to fit the 4096-byte field limit. Where Base64 is needed, it is applied before the CRLF escaping.
sections.eli5: If you want to write down something extra, you put a label on it, say how long it is, and then write it. Weird characters get turned into plain letters first.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows several optional fields for a 180 Ringing response. The Contact header is logged as 00@00000000,001C,00,Contact: <sip:bob@192.0.2.4> and the Reason-Phrase as 00@00000000,0016,00,Reason-Phrase: Ringing.

An SDP body of 123 bytes with Content-Type application/sdp gives a Value of 139 bytes, written in hexadecimal as 008B. A vendor field uses a vendor's own number. The RFC uses the documentation Private Enterprise Number 32473, for example 03@00032473,0014,00,a=rtpmap:0 PCMU/8000 for codec information.

Section 5 of the RFC then walks through an INVITE sent over TCP and the single record it would produce, with the index line starting A000100, followed by the tab-separated fields. It also supplies a Base64 copy of the exact bytes and a short perl script to decode it.
sections.eli5: The examples show real-looking entries so you can see how a message turns into a line of tidy, tab-separated facts.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
The document says it adds no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 6872. That RFC notes that values might need to be obfuscated for privacy when SIP CLF files are exchanged between domains. If a Base64 encoded string holds a non-obfuscated value, it also has to be obfuscated before Base64 encoding.

On operations, log files can use a lot of disk space depending on traffic and what is logged. Anyone using SIP CLF should set up file rollover procedures, but detailed operational guidelines are out of scope. The IANA section creates a registry for SIP CLF Version values (A is registered here) and one for Transport Flag values (U for UDP, T for TCP, S for SCTP).
sections.eli5: Logs can hold private details, so hide them before sharing, and remember to start new log files so the old ones do not fill up the disk.
